S&P 500 Thermometer

Objective. Investors watch dozens of indicators every day: the RSI, the 200-day moving average, the VIX, the CAPE, the yield curve… Each comes with a popular rule ("low RSI, a rebound is due"; "inverted curve, a recession is coming"). This study tests 26 indicators against what the S&P 500 actually did afterwards, over 1, 6 and 12 months and 3, 5 and 10 years, with data since 1928 (and since 1881 for valuation).

Result. In the short term, practically no indicator has predictive power. Out of correlations, look "significant" with a naive test, but about would be expected by pure chance. After correcting for multiple comparisons, remain, and only also pass a test that counts only non-overlapping periods. None of these survivors is a technical indicator: the RSI, the MACD, Bollinger Bands, the stochastic, moving-average crossovers and "buying the dip" say nothing reliable about future returns, on any timeframe.

What does emerge, in line with the academic literature, is that valuation matters in the long run. The most robust indicator is Shiller's equity premium over bonds (ECY): the higher it was, the better the returns over the following 5 and 10 years. The CAPE and the P/E point in the same direction, although with so few independent decades they do not pass every test. On the trend side, being below the 200-session or the 10-month average was followed by somewhat weaker returns, which is what trend followers argue.

Current situation. Stocks are expensive relative to their own history: the CAPE is at percentile (higher than in % of previous months) and the premium over bonds at percentile (a low premium means stocks offer little more than a bond). Historically, from such levels the market rose less than usual over the following 5-10 years, but it did not always fall, and these data cannot tell when an adjustment will come.

What survives the tests

Only results that pass the multiple-comparison correction and the conservative test on non-overlapping periods (marked solid). The rest of the report also shows hints, which only pass the first one.

Map of all indicators

Spearman correlation between the indicator value and the subsequent return. Blue: higher value, higher return. Red: higher value, lower return. The arrow shows what the popular belief expects. ● = solid result; ○ = hint. Hover over each cell for the confidence interval and p-values. Valuation and macro data are published monthly and are only analysed on monthly data.

Short term: 1 to 10 days

This is the horizon at which the RSI, the 2-period RSI and Bollinger Bands are actually used. Over the whole history, they predict nothing in the S&P: their correlations with the return over the next 1, 5 and 10 sessions are zero. Out of correlations, are solid, but they are tiny effects that only show up because of the large amount of data: the trend (being above the 200 average, and momentum) and, above all, the VIX. When fear in the market was high, the following two weeks were somewhat better than average, and the effect is stronger in the second half of the history than in the first.

The table by period shows something the average hides: the behaviour has changed sign. Until the 1970s there was some short-term momentum; in the last decade it is the opposite, and the index tends to rebound after falling. In 2013-2026, after an RSI (14) below 30, the S&P was higher 10 sessions later 71% of the time, against 64% for that period. That is the direction of the popular rule, although with the cases of a single decade it cannot be confirmed statistically. It is the opposite of Bitcoin, where following the rise is what worked.

Same analysis and tests, using daily bars against the return over the next 1, 5 and 10 bars. ● = solid; ○ = hint.

Does it still work today?

A signal can be solid over the whole history and still have faded in recent years. Each rule by period: % of times the price was higher at the end of the horizon, against the average for that same period. ● = significant difference in that period (binomial test on non-overlapping cases, p < 0.05). With few cases per period, most differences do not reach significance even if they exist.

Valuation: 145 years of history

Robert Shiller's data go back to 1881 and allow measuring the total real return (with dividends and net of inflation), which is what an investor actually receives. Each point is a month: horizontally, the valuation in that month; vertically, the annual real return over the following 10 years. The orange line marks where we are today.

All on equal terms: since 1990

Each indicator has a history of different length (the VIX starts in 1990 and the CAPE in the 19th century). To compare them fairly, here they are all measured over the same period, from 1990 to today, on monthly data.

How it was done

Data

  • S&P 500: daily closes from Yahoo Finance (^GSPC) since 30 December 1927. Until March 1957 the series is its 90-stock predecessor. Real highs and lows only since 1962.
  • VIX: Yahoo Finance (^VIX), since 1990.
  • Interest rates, credit, inflation, unemployment, production, financial conditions, GDP and corporate market value: FRED, the St. Louis Federal Reserve database.
  • Earnings, dividends and CPI since 1871: Robert Shiller's dataset (Irrational Exuberance).

No look-ahead

Every data point is used only from the moment it could have been known. This is the most common mistake in this kind of analysis, and it is handled as follows:

DataWhen it is publishedWhen it is used from
S&P 500 and VIX pricesAt the daily closeThat same close. If the market is open when downloading, the current session is discarded.
Interest rates (monthly averages)At the end of the monthDay 1 of the following month
CPI, unemployment, industrial productionDuring the following monthDay 1 of the second following month
Earnings and dividends (Shiller)Weeks after the quarter closes4 months after the month they refer to
GDP and Z.1 market valueAbout 10 weeks after the quarter6 months after the start of the quarter
10-year − 2-year spreadThe next dayThe next day
Financial conditions (NFCI)On the Wednesday after the week7 days after the reference Friday

The zones of each indicator (quintiles) are computed at each date using only the previous history and require 10 years of prior data. Using quintiles from the whole series would introduce look-ahead bias: a CAPE of 25 was very expensive in 1950 and normal in 2010.

Measures

  • Future return: from the close of each bar to the last known close at the target date (on monthly bars, exactly N months later). It is a price return, without dividends, except in Shiller's long history, which is total and real.
  • Spearman correlation: uses the ranks of the values rather than their magnitude, so it is not affected by outliers or by non-linear relationships.
  • Zones and rules: % of times the S&P was higher at the end of the horizon, and average return, compared with the average over the same period.
  • Events (crossovers, first yield-curve inversion, first 20% drawdown…): each one is counted once. Only events at least one horizon apart are used in the statistical test.

Statistical tests

  • Circular block bootstrap with blocks the size of the horizon: it accounts for the overlap of long-horizon returns (two consecutive months share 119 of 120 months at 10 years). A textbook formula would make almost everything "significant".
  • Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons, separately for correlations, zones and events. With correlations and zones, 5% would come out significant by chance.
  • Conservative test: repeats the test counting only non-overlapping periods (a t-test with as many degrees of freedom as independent periods; for zones, an exact binomial test on separated observations). It addresses the critique by Boudoukh, Richardson and Whitelaw (2008) on "long-horizon predictability".
  • Levels: solid passes the multiple-comparison correction and the conservative test; hint only the first; the rest, no evidence.
  • Everything is reproducible: the bootstrap uses a fixed seed and the code is in src/, with automated tests in src/pruebas.test.mjs.

Limitations

  • There is less history than it seems. In 98 years there are only 9 non-overlapping 10-year periods. Any conclusion at 5-10 years rests on a handful of decades.
  • Revised data. FRED provides the latest version of each series, not the one known at the time. Unemployment and industrial production are revised little; the NFCI index is re-estimated in full every week, so its history may be more accurate than it was in real time, and its results should be read with caution.
  • A single market. The US S&P 500 was one of the best markets of the 20th century (country survivorship bias). What worked here may not work elsewhere.
  • Price return. Except in the long history, dividends are not included. This does not change the comparison between zones, but it makes rises look less frequent than they really were.
  • No costs or taxes. This measures associations, not strategies. A rule that "works" may stop working after fees, taxes and the fact that many people use it.
  • Not investment advice. This is a historical analysis for educational purposes.

Next step

Combine the indicators with some evidence in a model (logistic regression) validated walk-forward: train on data up to a given year, predict the next one and move the window forward, to see whether the combination beats the base rate out of sample.
